newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says confessed spy cooperated fully.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says confessed spy cooperated fully.

text.p: Confessed double-agent Harold Nicholson should serve just under 24 years in prison because he has "substantially" helped gauge the harm caused by his sellout to Moscow, federal prosecutors have recommended.
Nicholson, 46, pleaded guilty on March 3 to conspiracy to commit espionage, the highest-ranking officer of the Central Intelligence Agency ever to face spy charges.
He was to be sentenced on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Alexandria, Virginia.

In a sentencing recommendation filed on Monday, the government said it believed Nicholson, a 16-year CIA veteran who uncloaked students he helped train for undercover missions, had cooperated fully with FBI and CIA debriefers.

Nicholson admitted collecting $300,000 from the Russians, rather than the $200,000 the government could prove, prosecutors said. They said the government had independently corroborated many of the other details Nicholson had provided since pleading guilty as part of a plea bargain.

"Nicholson has fully cooperated and substantially assisted the United States, and a sentence greater than 283 months could, in effect, be a life sentence," the prosecutors said. "In light of Nicholson's earnest, complete and substantial post-plea assistance (23 years and seven) months is a sufficient and appropriate punishment for his crime."

Nicholson has confessed to having started spying in June 1994, four months after Aldrich Ames, a lower-ranking CIA officer, was uncovered as a Russian spy. He acknowledged that he met his Russian handlers four times -- in India, Indonesia, Switzerland and Singapore -- to sell classified U.S. national security secrets.

After initially pleading not guilty to working for Moscow, he agreed to help assess the damage his sellout had done to avoid life imprisonment or a possible death sentence if convicted in a jury trial.

Jonathan Shapiro, one of two court-appointed co-lead defence counsels, said he would ask District Judge James Cacheris to give Nicholson even less time -- 21 years and 10 months -- the minimum he could hope for under the plea deal.

"We're hoping that the judge will consider (Nicholson's) significant work for the country over the last 20 years," Shapiro said in an interview at his office on Tuesday. "He did a whole lot before taking this turn."

The acting director of central intelligence, George Tenet, said in a letter to Cacheris that Nicholson's sellout had seriously damaged the CIA's ability to perform its mission and safeguard its undercover operatives.

"Mr Nicholson revealed or planned to reveal the names and positions of a large number of CIA officers whose jobs depend on their ability to work clandestinely," Tenet wrote. He said some had been working under "our deepest cover program" and had to be withdrawn because their lives were at risk.
Tenet said Nicholson's espionage had forced the CIA to abort promising intelligence missions and left permanent uncertainty about the contribution he had made to Russian spy operations.

Nicholson is a divorced father of three. He served as CIA station chief in Romania from 1990 to 1992 before becoming deputy chief of station and operations in Malaysia. Earlier, he was posted to the Philippines, Thailand and Japan.
